WASHINGTON, Feb. 11.

"CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas,

January 15, 1846.

"I perceive that some of the northern papers contain statements in regard to the sickness and so called hardships of the army here which are calculated to produce false impressions, and perhaps do mischief. There has been, at no time, what may be called extraordinary sickness in our camp. Some of the regiments—particularly the 5th—were obliged to undergo a process of acclimation which, without creating mortality, necessarily made heavy sick report. Again the command suffered from dysentery, a disease common to large camps. These causes, together with our first inclement weather, brought the sick report, in the middle of November, to about 5 per cent of the total present. From that time until the present, although we have had much rain and severe weather, the report has gradually decreased, until it is now rather less than 10 per cent. Great attention has been paid to the comfort and well-being of the men by the regimental officers, and the hospitals have been subject to especial care. Some discomforts have necessarily been encountered, but the army has suffered nothing like hardships. It is encampment on soil particularly dry, the tents are protected from the north winds by embankments or thick hedges, the fuel is of excellent quality, and the supplies of every description for the use of the men are abundant and of good quality. Our fresh beef is particularly excellent, and the troops supply themselves at will with fresh fish. Thus you see there is no cause of complaint; and only regret that any one here should furnish statements so wide of the truth:

We have been unfortunate in the loss of several officers; but in almost every case the disease or debility was contracted elsewhere. Such was particularly the case with Lt. Col. Hartman, who came here in opposition to the advice of his physician. Several officers have been permitted to leave on the certificate of the surgeon that a change of climate was necessary. Our officers are quite healthy now.

The heavy details required for procuring fuel, &c., since the cold weather set in have to some extent, caused a suspension of the instruction; but it has been generally resumed since the new year, except in the light artillery, where it is physically impossible, with their small organization, to procure fuel and hay from considerable distance, and still continue instruction. It is pity to see that fine arm, so well appointed, almost paralyzed by its feeble numbers. The battalion of light artillery is in excellent order and capital of officers, hope it will be kept up to the establishment, which ought to be greatly increased.

Our bridge organization works very well, and gives the officers all opportunity of seeing duty done on larger scale than usual. Gen. Taylor retains the immediate command of the camp.

Sun wak'd forest,
Bird, that soarest,
O'er the mute empurpled moor,
Throstle's song, that stream-like flowest,
Wind, that over dew drop goest,
Welcome now the woe worn poor.

Little river,
Young for ever still,
Cloud, gold bright with thankful glee,
Happy woodbine, gladly weeping,
Gnat, within the wild-rose keeping,
That they were blessed as ye!

Sabbath holy
For the lowly still

Paint with flowers thy glittering sod
For Affection's sons and daughters,
Bid thy mountains, woods and waters,
Pray to God, the poor man's God!

Where, on Hope wants bars the door,
From the gloom of airless alleys,
Lead thou to green hills and valleys,
Where weary Lord lands trampled poor.

Pale young mother,
Gasping brother,
Sister toiling in despair,
Grief-bow'd sire, that life long diest,
White lipp'd child, that sleeping slightest,
Come and drink the light and air.

Tyrants curse ye, while they nurse ye,
Life for deadliest wrongs to pay;
Yet, oh, Sabbath! bringing gladness
Unto hearts of weary sadness,
And still thou art, The Poor Man's Day.

Alice arrived at a great experience. The meeting was to be held in one of the churches.

Her friend, who had become enthusiastic in the cause, urged her to go to this meeting, which Alice did, although with a feeling of reluctance. The house was crowded, above and below. The preliminaries usually appertaining to such meetings having been arranged, a brief opening address was made by one of the ministers. A reformed man then related his experience with great effect. After he had finished, there was a pause of nearly a minute. At length a man, who had been seated far back, with his face partly turned from the audience, arose slowly and moved to the front of the stage.

A half suppressed exclamation escaped Alice as her eyes caught the well known features of him who had been her husband, while a quick thrill ran through her. Then her whole frame trembled in accord with her fluttering heart. The face of Mr. Delaney was greatly changed since she had last looked upon it. Its calm, dignified elevation had been restored, but with what difference—what before was cheerful was sad, very sad.

"Mr. President, he began in subdued voice, although I had consented at your urgent solicitation, to address this large assembly to-night, yet I have felt so strong a reluctance to doing so, that it has been with the utmost difficulty I could drag myself forward. But I had passed my word, I could not violate it. As to relating my experience, that I do not think I can venture upon. The past days I do not recall. I only know that just ten years of my life were blotted out."

The speaker paused a moment, already much affected. Then, resuming in a firmer voice, said:

"But something must be said of my own case, or I shall fail to make that impression on your minds that I wish to produce."

Pictures of real life touch the heart with power, while abstract presentations of truth glitter coldly in the intellectual regions of the mind, and then fade from the perception like dissolving figures in the diorama.

Your speaker once stood among the first members of the legislature in the neighboring State. Nay, more than that—represented his country for three years in the Assembly of the Commonwealth. And more than that still—occupied a seat in Congress for two Congressional periods.

At this announcement, the stiffness of death pervaded the crowded assembly.

"And yet more than all that," he continued, his voice sinking into a low thrilling tone—"I once had a tenderly loved wife, and two sweet children. All these honors, all these blessings have departed from him," he continued, his voice growing louder and deeper in his effort to control himself. "He was unworthy to retain them. It threw him off because he had debased himself, and disgraced them. And worse of all—she who had borne him two dear babes, was forced to abandon, and seek an asylum in her house. And why? Could I become so changed in a few short years? What power was there so to abase me that my fellow-beings spurned, and even the wife of my bosom turned away, heart stricken from me? Alas! my friends, it was a most indulgence in mockery! I might have been the beastial, but for this, and were now an honorable and useful representative in Congress, pursuing after my country's good, and blessed in the home circle with wife and children. But I have not told you all. After my wife separated from me, I sank rapidly. A state of perfect misery briefly brought too many terrible thoughts; I therefore drank more freely, and was rarely if ever free from under the bewildering effects of partial intoxication. I remained in the same village for some years, but never once saw her during that time; nor a glimpse of my children. At last I became so abandoned in my life, that my wife, urged on by her friends, no doubt ill at ease, made an application for divorce; and as cause could readily be shown why it should be granted, a separation was legally declared. To complete my disgrace, at the next Congressional census I was left off the ticket as unfit to represent the district; I then left the country and State, where I had lived from my boyhood up.

Be it enacted by the General Assembly, of the State of Ohio, That whenever three or more persons, residents of any county, or district embracing two counties of this State, shall organize themselves into a society for the Improvement of Agriculture within said county or district, and shall have adopted a constitution and bylaws, agreeable to the rules and regulations to be furnished by the Ohio State Board of Agriculture hereafter created, and shall have appointed the usual and proper officers; and when the said society shall have raised and paid to the Treasurer, by voluntary subscription, or by fees imposed upon its members, any sum of money in each year, not less than fifty dollars; and whenever the President of said society shall certify to the respective county auditors, the amount thus paid, attested by the oath of the Treasurer, it shall be the duty of the said county Auditor embraced within the district in which such society shall be organized, to draw an order on the Treasurer of the respective counties, in favor of the President and Treasurer of said society, for a sum equal to the amount thus raised, provided, it does not exceed half a cent to each inhabitant of the said county, upon the basis of the last previous national census, but no more to exceed in any county the sum of two hundred dollars; and it shall be the duty of the Treasurer of the said county to pay the same.

Sec. 2. That it shall be the duty of the several county or district societies which may be formed under the provisions of the preceding section, during the continuance of this act, annually to offer and award premiums for the Improvement of soils, tillage, crops, manures, implements, stock, articles of domestic industry, and such other articles, productions and improvements, as they may deem proper; and may perform all such acts as they may deem best calculated to promote the agricultural and household manufacturing interest of the district and of the State; and it shall also be their duty, so to regulate the amount of premiums and the different grades of the same, so that it shall be competent for small as well as large farmers to have an opportunity to compete therefore; and in making their awards, special reference shall be had to the profits which may accrue or be likely to accrue from the improved mode of raising the crop, or of improving the soil, or stock, or of the fabrication of the articles thus offered, with the intention that the premium shall be given for the most economical mode of improvement; and all persons offering to compete for premiums on improved modes of tillage, or of the productions of any crops or other articles, shall be required before such premiums are adjudged to deliver to the awarding committee a full and correct statement of the process of such mode of tillage or production, and the nature and amount of the costs, with a view of showing accurately the profits derived or expected to be derived therefrom.

From the New York Tribune.


THE NEW TARIFF AT WORK.


Although the New Tariff does not take effect
until December, its influences already begin to be
felt. Are they good or evil! Let each citizen
carefully observe and candidly judge. Those
influences, whether for good or ill, will be gradually
developed and will naturally be somewhat
diversified. Some will perhaps be benefited,
others will certainly be injured. We believe
the latter will be by far the greater number so far
as our own people are concerned. We learn
that, on the news reaching England of the passage
of McKay's bill through the House, Iron advanced
there very considerably and the Iron business
assumed an air of cheerful activity.
There was something like this in British Manchester,
and in Havana the merchants and planters talked of
erecting a statue of gold to Secretary Walker. We
have not yet heard of any class of our own laborers
having occasion or feeling impelled to do anything of
the sort. When they do, we shall promptly announce it.
As it is indeed an ill wind that blows nobody any
good, we must presume that some class of our
people who earn their living by labor will be
benefited by the New Tariff. But that the greatest
happiness to the greatest number will be promoted
by its passage, we do not, cannot believe.


How those branches of Home Industry which
are directly discriminated against by this Tariff are
to thrive under it, we cannot yet discover. Our
earnest inquiries of the advocates of this measure
are met by profound silence, or rather instead of
giving us any answer to our plain, pertinent and
practical inquiry, they devote their energies and
columns to such ends as these: 1st, Fulminations
of threats that if the Manufacturers don't lie still
the Tariff shall be repealed altogether, and Direct
Taxation resorted to for the support of the Government;
2d, Inquiries if thirty per cent. isn't Protection enough,
when half our rivaled interests are exposed to foreign
competition at less than that to less than nothing;
and 3d, Defamation against the enormous profits to
Manufacturers hitherto and the high salaries paid to
Presidents, Agents, &c. of Manufacturing Companies,
with assurances that if these are placed on proper
footing, the works can all go on and make fair profits,
even under the Tariff just passed.


To these representations, we would briefly
make answer, Messrs. Free Traders, if you wish
to risk yourselves on fair trial of your theory
by repeating the Tariff wholly and collecting the
taxes. We, surely, have now no power to hinder
you, and we ask nothing from your compassion.
We dare we defy you to show that you have
any confidence in your own doctrines. If the
basis of Walker's Report and every plausible argument
on your side be not utterly unsound, then the
change you threaten would be the best thing
possible for our People generally. We think it
would produce great mischief and suffering, but
we do not believe it could possibly continue two
years, and we believe the scary lesson of experience
would be worth even its very cost.

genuine Free Trade! Let us see five cry you
mercy and if you make anything by the experience.

and the facility of going on under the New Tariff,
we have only this to say, Gentlemen Free Traders!
all we want is to have Home Manufacturers go on
prosperously, our goods which well can be made at
home, and our own laborers fairly paid. Now if any
of the present manufacturers stop business or slack off,

pay full wages, and you will be sure of the best and
most efficient workers in every department. If they
pay too high salaries to officers, do you avoid that
error and pocket the saving; if they have been making
great profits, your chance for fair profits is the better.

it and show your faith that it will work well. If

ampler markets for our Farmers' produce, more work

Joseph Err of Jacob Ler deed VS. the Croioh Co.—Action to recover $4,000 alleged to have been insured in three policies on buildings in Bond and Market which were burnt at the great fire in July, 1845.

Publicity has just been given to an interesting fact, connected with the repulse and defeat of the British at New Orleans, in 1814.

Those who are old enough to remember the war of 1812, may recollect remarkable instances of bravery in the defence of the American privateer, General Armstrong, Capt. Samuel C. Reed, which was attacked while lying in the harbor of Fayal, in the Western Islands by the boats of three of the enemy's ships of war, consisting of the Rofa frigate, the Piscogenet, and the Commodore brig, on the 26th September, 1814, in which engagement, out of the attacking force, nearly four hundred strong, the British lost between two and three hundred, killed and wounded, while on the part of the Americans, only two were killed and seven wounded. Remember the sensation which this news produced on its arrival in our seaport cities, as one of the most brilliant exploits in naval warfare.

It now seems, and the fact is abundantly sustained by documentary evidences, that this engagement, with its results, delayed Admiral Lloyd, who had charge of the squadron above alluded to, ten days at Fayal, whence he sent the severely wounded home to England on the Thracis and Calypso ships of war. He then proceeded to Jamaica, where Admiral Cochrane and General Packenham had been waiting for him several days, who were highly indignant at this delay, and loaded him with bitter reproaches. Well nigh, they have done so if they could have foreseen the fruits of that ten days' delay! Cochrane's fleet of eighty-six sail of vessels arrived at the mouth of the Mississippi on the 9th December, 1814. Gen. Jackson had reached New Orleans on the 5th, only four days before. The Kentucky and Tennessee troops did not arrive until the 10th, nor were they fully supplied with arms and especially gun flints, until a later date. It therefore, the invading fleet and army, had arrived ten or twelve days sooner, say on the 25th November, when was there to improvise the slightest impediment to their conquest and sack of that beautiful city of New Orleans, destitute of military forces or defences, and population hardly long enough part of an American community to possess the requisite spirit and patriotism for resistance.

It opened the session to-day in the consideration of the amendments proposed to the bill necessary to the act providing for the prosecution of the war with Mexico. The debate, of which we have a full report, had reference mainly to the question of selecting the additional field officers required for their period of service. Without acting on these amendments, the Senate, at an advanced hour of the afternoon, went into executive session.

The atmosphere there was extremely oppressive. It would appear that the new ventilator does not work very well; senators complained much of the circulation of vitiated air in the chamber, of which the occupants of the reporters gallery had an ample share.

Mr. Blair proposed to call up the joint resolution, which he had yesterday introduced, rendering the thanks of Congress to General Taylor and the army of occupation for the recent successes on the Rio Grande; but he withdrew the motion, on an intimation by Mr. Harlan that it would be better to wait the arrival of communication which probably might be expected from the President of the United States, transmitting the official dispatches of the general in command.

The House then immediately passed into Committee of the Whole on the state of the Union, and resumed the consideration of the civil and diplomatic appropriation bill. A heavy debate followed, a large part of which was purely of local character, and possessing no general interest. the Arkansas. He reports that Armijo had
been suspended as Governor to Santa Fe,
and Gen. UREA appointed in his place; and
that the most rigorous steps were taken to
prepare for a war of defence or offence; that
notifications and military preparations of va-
rious kinds were going on; the draught
was actively progressing in Santa Fe and
Chihuahua, and that every third man of the
whole population was taken. The Indians
were reported to be unfavourable to the A-
mericans, and the Mexicans relied much on
their aid. Gen. UREA has dispatched 800
troops to march to Bent's Fort, and to meet
Spier's company on the prairies, and conduct
it into Santa Fe. This was the company
that was said to have taken quantity of
arms and ammunition to Santa Fe, and in
pursuit of which Col. KEARNEY had sent the
United States Dragoons. Mr. Bransford
states that it would be impossible for the
Dragoons to overtake them before they would
arrive at Santa Fe. Mr. B. expressed the
opinion very confidently that before that time
Bent's Fort would be in the possession of
the Mexicans.


The Randor left Fort Leavenworth on
Monday last. At that time nine volunteer
companies had arrived at the Fort. All the
regular troops had started over the prairies
except thirty or forty. The volunteer com-
panies from the upper country are said to
embrace a large number of bold, rough, un-
governable spirits, who delight in the largest
liberty; and it is found exceedingly difficult
to subject them to military discipline. Col.
Kearney has much trouble in keeping order,
and will probably find more difficult to disci-
pline some of the Missouri volunteers than to
conquer New Mexico. The absence of the
regular troops and officers renders it more
difficult to enforce discipline or teach military
tactics.
